reading.heading: Features and benefits
reading.explanation:
A **feature** is what a product has or is: "a 20-hour battery", "made of steel", "free delivery". A **benefit** is what that feature does for the customer: "use it all week without charging", "it will last for years", "no trip to the shop".

People buy benefits, because benefits answer the question "What’s in it for me?"

To find one, take each feature and ask **"So what?"** until you reach something the customer actually feels:
- saved time
- saved money
- less stress
- more pleasure.

Good copy usually names the benefit first and uses the feature as the proof.

reading.heading: One big idea
reading.explanation:
Strong advertising says **one thing clearly** rather than ten things weakly. That one thing is often written as a **value proposition**:
- what you offer
- who it is for
- why it is better, in one sentence.

"Healthy lunches delivered in ten minutes for busy students."

Before writing, ask: if the reader remembers only one thing, what should it be? Then make every headline, image and sentence support that idea.

Extra messages are not free: each one makes the main idea harder to see. If everything is important, nothing is.

reading.heading: Headlines that work
reading.explanation:
A **headline** has one job: to make the right reader want to read the next line. Most strong headlines do at least one of these things:
- promise a clear benefit
- ask a question the reader cares about
- give a specific number
- share something new.

"Cut your energy bill by a third this winter" works better than "Great savings!" because it is specific and believable.

Write for one reader, keep it short and use concrete words. Avoid empty praise words such as great, best and amazing unless you can prove them. Write ten versions and choose the clearest, not the cleverest.

reading.heading: Honest claims
reading.explanation:
Advertising **must be true**, and in many countries the law requires it. Do not:
- claim what you cannot prove
- hide important costs
- invent reviews.

If results vary, say so: "up to 30% faster", "results vary". Keep evidence ready for every factual claim. Be careful with **absolute words** — best, only, never, guaranteed — because each one is a promise you must keep.

Honest copy is not weaker copy. Specific, true details are more persuasive than exaggeration, and trust brings customers back.

reading.heading: A short ad with AIDA
reading.explanation:
**AIDA** is a simple plan for short ads, posts and emails.
- **Attention**: a strong headline or image that stops the right reader.
- **Interest**: a fact, question or short story that fits their situation.
- **Desire**: show the benefit and how life improves, with proof.
- **Action**: say exactly what to do next.

Each part should be short and lead naturally to the next. AIDA is not a formula to fill in mechanically; it is a check that you have taken the reader from noticing to acting.

examples.answer: Tired of cold coffee by 10 a.m.?
Our steel mug keeps drinks hot for 6 hours, so your second cup tastes like the first.
Order today — free delivery this week.

reading.heading: Calls to action
reading.explanation:
A **call to action** (CTA) tells the reader exactly what to do next. Start it with a strong, specific verb:
- Book
- Try
- Join
- Download
- Start.

"Book your free class" is clearer than "Click here", because it says what the click does. Add a reason or a time limit if it is real: "Start your free 14-day trial", "Register by Friday to save 20%".

Use **one main CTA** per message; several competing buttons make people hesitate. Place it where the reader is ready to decide, and repeat it on long pages.

reading.heading: Voice and tone
reading.explanation:
**Tone** is how your words sound to the reader: friendly, serious, playful, expert, calm. Choose a tone that fits both the audience and the product, and keep it consistent across the website, emails and packaging.

Write as if you are talking to **one person**: use "you", short words and natural sentences. A bank and a skateboard shop can both be friendly, but in different ways. Never be rude, and never talk down to people.

Read your copy aloud: if it sounds like a real person speaking to you, the tone is probably right.

Your account has been locked to protect your data.

reading.heading: Editing for clarity
reading.explanation:
Most copy gets better by **getting shorter**. Cut words that do not add meaning:
- "in order to" → "to"
- "really very unique" → "unique".

Replace vague words with **concrete ones**:
- "fast" → "ready in five minutes"
- "affordable" → "from £9 a month".

Use active verbs and short sentences. Then read it aloud; wherever you stumble, rewrite. Check facts, names, prices and links last, when your eyes are fresh.

A useful final test: **one idea, one reader, one action**.

reading.heading: Learning from your reader
reading.explanation:
Good copy starts with **the reader’s words**, not the company’s. Read:
- reviews
- support emails
- survey answers
- forum posts.

Look for the problems people describe and the phrases they repeat. A review like "The light is soft, so my eyes don’t hurt at night" tells you the benefit that really matters.

Use those words in your headlines and benefits; they sound true because they are how customers already think. Complaints are useful too: they show the doubts your copy must answer.

reading.heading: Proof makes claims believable
reading.explanation:
Any claim is easier to believe with **proof**. The main kinds are:
- numbers ("4.6 stars from 1,200 buyers")
- guarantees ("30-day free returns")
- short customer quotes with a name
- independent tests or awards
- demonstrations (a photo or video showing it working).

Be specific: "1,200 buyers" beats "thousands of happy customers". Put the proof next to the claim it supports.

**Never invent proof.** If you have little proof, claim less and be honest about what you can show.

reading.heading: Answering the reader’s doubts
reading.explanation:
Before people buy, they have **doubts**:
- Is it worth the price?
- Will it work for me?
- What if I don’t like it?
- Will it arrive in time?

Good copy answers the doubts it can, honestly and near the moment of decision. Use a short "Questions" section, a line near the button ("Free returns for 30 days"), or a comparison.

If there is a real limitation, say it and offer a solution: "The cable is short, so we include a 2-metre extension." Honesty about small weaknesses makes the strong claims more believable.

reading.heading: A mini-story in copy
reading.explanation:
A very short story can sell an idea faster than a list of features. Use **a person, a problem and a change**, in two or three sentences: "Mira worked late and her eyes hurt. She switched to a soft-light lamp. Now she finishes the day without a headache."

Make the person like your reader, keep the details real, and end on the benefit, followed by the next step.

Stories **must be true** or clearly presented as examples; an invented "customer story" presented as real is misleading.

reading.heading: Subject lines and short emails
reading.explanation:
In email, the **subject line** decides whether the message is opened. Keep it short (about 6–8 words), specific and honest: "Free shipping until Friday" is better than "Amazing offer!!!".

Use the reader’s name sparingly, and never trick people with "Re:" or fake urgency — it damages trust and deliverability.

In the **body**:
- put the main message in the first lines
- use short paragraphs
- give one clear button or link.

Write as one person to another, and make it easy to unsubscribe.

reading.heading: A page that sells

A **landing page** works best when it follows the questions in the reader’s head, in order.
- Start with a clear headline and one line saying who it is for.
- Then show the main benefits, the proof, and answers to common doubts.
- End with one clear action, and repeat the button where decisions happen.

Use headings so people can scan, short paragraphs, and an image that shows the product in use. Remove anything that distracts from the **single goal** of the page, including extra links.

reading.heading: Testing one change
reading.explanation:
Copywriters **test ideas** instead of arguing about them. In an **A/B test**, half the readers see version A and half see version B.

**Change only one thing** — the headline, the button text or the image — so you know what caused the difference. Decide in advance what counts as success, such as more sign-ups, not just more clicks.

Wait until enough people have seen each version; a result from twenty readers is often just chance. Keep a record of what you tested and learned, so the team does not repeat old tests.

reading.heading: Honest urgency and fine print
reading.explanation:
**Urgency** gives a real reason to act now. "Sale ends Friday" is honest if the sale really ends on Friday; "Only 3 left" must be true. Fake countdown timers and invented scarcity destroy trust and may break consumer rules.

Put important conditions in **plain words close to the offer**, not hidden in small print: "Free shipping on orders over $40." Clear terms reduce complaints and refunds, and they make the offer itself more believable.

reading.heading: Positioning: one proposition
reading.explanation:
**Positioning** is the place a brand holds in the customer’s mind compared with alternatives. Find the **single proposition** that is:
- true
- relevant to the customer
- different from competitors: the one reason to choose you.

A brand that tries to be best at everything is remembered for nothing.

A useful form is: **For [audience] who [need], [brand] is the [category] that [key difference].** "For commuters who depend on their bike, Harbor is the repair shop that fixes it overnight." Every ad then supports that sentence.

The only bank that answers calls in under a minute.

reading.heading: Brand voice and consistency
reading.explanation:
A brand speaks in many places: ads, packaging, emails, app messages, even error screens. A **voice guide** keeps it recognisable. It usually contains:
- a few adjectives for the voice (calm, practical, a little dry)
- words to prefer and avoid
- examples.

**Voice stays the same; tone changes** with the moment — serious for an apology, lighter for a welcome.

A quick test: cover the logo. Could the copy belong to any brand? If so, sharpen the voice.

reading.heading: Long copy that keeps momentum
reading.explanation:
**Long copy** works when readers are making a serious decision: an expensive product, a course, a service they will use for years. It must keep earning the next sentence.

Open with the strongest hook, name a clear problem, then move through:
- benefits
- proof
- objections
- the offer.

Use subheadings so readers can scan and re-enter, short paragraphs, and sentences that begin with the reader’s concerns. End each section with a reason to read on, and cut anything that does not move the reader toward the decision.

reading.heading: Using persuasion honestly
reading.explanation:
Research describes common patterns in decisions:
- People follow what others do (**social proof**),
- feel losses more strongly than equal gains (**loss aversion**),
- judge value by comparison (**anchoring**).

These patterns can help you communicate clearly — or can mislead. Use them honestly:
- show real numbers of real customers
- describe a real cost of waiting
- compare with a fair alternative.

A simple test: if you would be uncomfortable explaining the technique to the customer, do not use it.

reading.heading: Taglines: rhythm and wordplay
reading.explanation:
A **tagline** is a short line a brand repeats for years. It should be easy to say and hard to forget.

**Rhythm** helps:
- short words
- a clear beat
- repetition
- alliteration
- a pair of contrasts.

Wordplay can make a line memorable when it clarifies the promise; it fails when readers have to work to understand it. "Back on the road by morning" promises a benefit in plain words.

Test a tagline aloud, test it with people who do not know the product, and make sure it is true.

reading.heading: Writing for other cultures
reading.explanation:
Words and images do not travel unchanged. **Translation** moves the meaning into another language; **transcreation** rebuilds the message so it works in the new culture.

A slogan that sounds lucky in one language may be rude, funny or flat in another. Colours, numbers, gestures, humour and holidays carry different meanings.

**Keep the proposition the same**, but adapt the expression, examples and images. Always check with people from the target culture, and plan time for local review before launch.

reading.heading: Substantiation and disclosure
reading.explanation:
Advertising claims must be **truthful and supported by evidence** you hold before you publish. "Clinically proven" needs a proper study and an accurate summary of it, not a small test presented as proof.

**Disclose important limits** clearly and close to the claim: sample size, "results vary", the conditions of an offer. Comparisons must compare like with like, and paid endorsements must be labelled as paid.

Rules differ by country, so follow your region’s rules and ask a qualified adviser. This is language practice, not legal advice.

reading.heading: Working from a brief
reading.explanation:
A **creative brief** tells you what the work must achieve. Read it for:
- the audience
- the problem
- the single message
- the proof
- the tone
- the practical limits: format, length, deadline.

Ask questions before you write: Who exactly? What should they do? What do they believe now?

When you present your copy, **link each choice back to the brief**: "Because commuters fear breaking down, the headline promises the next morning." Take feedback on the work, not on yourself, and revise toward the brief rather than toward personal taste.

archivedLessons.title: Persuasion principles, used honestly
archivedLessons.tip: Research describes patterns in decisions: people follow what others do (social proof), dislike losses more than they like equal gains (loss aversion), and judge by comparison (anchoring). archivedLessons.title: Taglines: rhythm and wordplay
archivedLessons.tip: A tagline is a short line that a brand repeats. It should be easy to say and hard to forget. Rhythm helps: short words, a clear beat, perhaps repetition or a pair of contrasts. Wordplay can be memorable when it clarifies; it fails when readers must work to understand it. “Back on the road by morning” promises a benefit in plain words. archivedLessons.tip: Words and images do not travel unchanged. Translation moves the meaning; transcreation rebuilds the message so that it works in the new culture. archivedLessons.title: Substantiation and disclosure
archivedLessons.tip: Advertising claims must be truthful and supported by evidence you hold before you publish. A claim such as “clinically proven” needs a proper study and an accurate summary, not a small test described as proof. Disclose material limits clearly near the claim: sample size, “results vary,” conditions of an offer. Comparative claims must compare like with like. Paid endorsements must be disclosed as such. Rules differ by country, so follow your region’s rules and ask a qualified adviser. This is language practice, not legal advice.

archivedLessons.title: Work from a brief
archivedLessons.tip: A brief tells you what the work must achieve. Read it for the audience, the problem, the single message, the proof, the tone and the practical limits (format, length, deadline). Ask questions before you write: Who exactly? What should they do? What do they believe now? When you present copy, link each choice to the brief: “Because commuters fear a breakdown, the headline promises the next morning.” Take feedback on the work, not on yourself, and revise toward the brief.
